analysis.one_liner: Extends Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes to income above $400,000 to fund the programs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on May 8, 2025 with 5 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises money for Social Security and Medicare by changing how high earners are taxed. Today, Social Security payroll tax stops applying to wages above a yearly cap, and investment income only pays a 3.8% Medicare tax. This bill would keep collecting the Social Security payroll tax on wages up to $400,000, add a new 1.2% Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000, and raise the Medicare tax on investment and business income of people making over $400,000 (or $500,000 for couples) from 3.8% to 17.4%. The new money would be deposited into the Social Security and Medicare trust funds that pay retirement, disability, and hospital benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries, because the bill directs all the new revenue into the program trust funds, and by extension every worker who relies on those benefits. The tax falls entirely on high-income individuals: it applies to wages between the annual Social Security wage cap and $400,000, wages above $400,000, and investment and business income of people making over $400,000 ($500,000 for joint filers).

how_it_helps.text: The bill keeps collecting the Social Security payroll tax on wages between the current annual wage cap and $400,000, instead of stopping at the cap, and applies the same rules to self-employment income and railroad retirement taxes.
The bill adds a new 1.2% Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers.

The bill raises the net investment income tax rate from 3.8% to 17.4% for people with income over the $400,000/$500,000 thresholds, and broadens it to cover certain business income that is currently excluded and to foreign income.
The bill directs 71.3% of the new investment-income tax revenue to the Social Security trust fund, 10.3% to the disability trust fund, and 28.7% to the Medicare hospital insurance trust fund.
The bill's stated purpose is to increase funding for Social Security and Medicare.
The bill applies to wages and taxable years beginning on or after the first January 1 after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with very high incomes. Employees earning more than the annual Social Security wage cap pay the tax on wages up to $400,000 and more; a new 1.2% tax applies above $400,000 (or $500,000 for couples); and people with investment or business income over those thresholds pay 17.4% instead of 3.8% on it. High-income self-employed people and owners of pass-through businesses face the largest changes, since the bill extends the Medicare tax to income that currently escapes it.

drawbacks.text: It is a large tax increase on high earners, roughly a 13.6 percentage point rise in the tax on investment and business income, which would face strong opposition and could encourage high earners to restructure income to avoid it.
The bill taxes wages above the Social Security wage cap without crediting those earnings toward higher benefits, decoupling the tax from the benefit formula that traditionally links the two.

Because the new investment-income tax applies to specified business income that was previously excluded, business owners would owe the tax on operating income even when it funds other obligations, adding compliance complexity.
The bill raises revenue for existing programs but does not itself expand any benefits, so its value to beneficiaries depends on the trust funds staying solvent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: dedicated revenue into the Social Security and Medicare trust funds reduces the pressure for future benefit cuts, and the cost falls only on households making over $400,000. The cost to those households is significant, especially the jump in the tax on investment and business income. The design is straightforward and targeted, though the lack of extra benefit credit above the wage cap and the breadth of the new business-income tax are honest objections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and sent to the Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote so far.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 8, 2025 by Senator Whitehouse, joined by Senators Klobuchar and Van Hollen.
On the day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The bill has 5 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The action history shows no steps beyond the initial referral: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action.

Today, Social Security payroll tax only applies to wages up to the annual contribution and benefit base, which is why the bill's first change is to extend taxation to wages between the cap and $400,000.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no final winner, because the bill is still pending. High-income households are better off with each week of inaction, since they continue paying Social Security tax only on wages under the annual cap and a 3.8% rather than 17.4% rate on investment income.

sides.party_line_note: All 6 Senate supporters of the bill are Democrats, and no Republican has cosponsored it; no one has acted to block or advance it since the referral to Finance.

industries.note: These taxpayers would pay Social Security tax on wages above the annual cap up to $400,000, a new 1.2% tax on wages above $400,000, and 17.4% instead of 3.8% on investment and business income. Their interest in stopping the bill runs against the program funding ordinary beneficiaries would gain.

industries.industry: Owners of pass-through businesses and investment funds
industries.note: The bill broadens the net investment income tax to cover business income that is currently excluded from it, so active business owners with income over the threshold would owe the higher tax on operating income, not just passive returns.

industries.industry: Social Security and Medicare trust funds and their beneficiaries
industries.note: The bill routes 71.3% of new investment-tax revenue to Social Security's retirement fund, 10.3% to disability, and 28.7% to Medicare hospital insurance, directly shoring up the programs beneficiaries rely on.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic cosponsors and no committee action since referral, the bill is unlikely to reach the Senate floor this Congress unless leadership schedules it; tax bills in the Finance Committee with no hearing or markup after months typically die without a vote.
